interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between backward and forward compatibility, and why do both matter in a real pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Backward compatibility means a new schema can read data written under an old schema — it protects you when consumers lag behind a producer's change. Forward compatibility is the reverse: an old schema can read data written under a new schema — it protects you when a producer ships before every consumer has upgraded.

Both matter because in any system with more than a couple of independently-deployed services, you can't guarantee upgrade order. If I only have backward compatibility and a producer ships a new field before a consumer upgrades, the old consumer might choke on the new shape — that's exactly the gap forward compatibility closes. Full compatibility, both directions at once, is what lets producers and consumers each deploy on their own schedule without a coordinated release, which is the realistic operating mode for most teams past a certain size.

A concrete example: adding an optional field with a default is backward compatible (new readers of old data get the default) and forward compatible (old readers of new data simply ignore the field they don't know about) — which is exactly why "add optional with default" is the textbook safe change, and why removing or renaming a field breaks one or both directions.

I'd configure the specific compatibility mode explicitly on the schema registry per topic, rather than relying on convention, so a breaking change gets rejected automatically instead of caught in a postmortem.

**Testing:** whether you know these are two distinct, directional guarantees, not synonyms for "compatible."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: A producer team wants to add a required field to an event schema because every new event genuinely should have it. How would you get them what they want without breaking existing consumers?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate the schema-level guarantee from the business-logic intent, because those are two different things that happen to look similar. Structurally, a required field with no default breaks immediately: old data and any consumer still on the previous schema have no value to fall back to, so deserialization fails outright.

What I'd actually do: add the field as optional with a sensible default — even a sentinel value that clearly signals "not present" if there's no natural default — so the change is backward and forward compatible on day one. That lets old data keep working and lets consumers upgrade on their own timeline.

Then I'd treat "required" as an application-layer guarantee, enforced going forward: validate at the producer that every *newly emitted* event includes it, and monitor the field's presence rate in the data. Once monitoring shows it's been present in 100% of events for long enough that no straggler old-schema producer is still running, I'd consider a second migration — potentially a true breaking change with a version bump and a coordinated consumer upgrade, which is now a deliberate, planned event instead of an accidental outage.

The pattern generalizes: schema compatibility rules are almost never the place to encode "this must always be present" — that belongs in validation and monitoring, layered on top of a schema that stays technically permissive.

**Testing:** whether you can reconcile a real business need with the schema's technical compatibility constraints, rather than picking one and ignoring the other.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: How does a schema registry actually enforce compatibility, and what happens mechanically when a producer tries to publish a breaking schema change?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A schema registry stores every version of every schema registered for a topic, along with a configured compatibility mode — backward, forward, full, or none — for that topic. When a producer client starts up or is about to publish with a new schema, it first registers that schema with the registry. The registry compares the proposed schema against the relevant prior version(s) using the topic's configured rule, and either accepts it, assigning it a new version number and schema ID, or rejects the registration outright with an error describing which field violated the rule.

Mechanically, this means the check happens before a single message is ever produced with the new schema — the producer's registration call fails, the application gets an exception, and no bad data reaches the topic at all. That's a meaningfully stronger guarantee than a code-review policy, because it's automatic and can't be skipped by an engineer in a hurry.

On the read side, each message is tagged with a small schema ID rather than the full schema, so consumers fetch the matching schema from the registry (usually cached after the first lookup) to deserialize — which is also why the registry has to stay available for the pipeline to function; it's a dependency, not just a governance nicety.

Concretely, if I tried to remove a field a topic's BACKWARD rule requires readers to still find, the registration call itself would fail with a clear error before deployment — that's the failure mode you want, caught in CI or a pre-deploy check, not in production.

**Testing:** whether you understand the registry as an enforcement mechanism with a specific request/response flow, not just an abstract "place schemas live."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Mechanism

interviewQuestions.question: You're ingesting data from a third-party API you don't control, and it periodically changes its response shape without warning. How do you protect your pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
With an external source, I accept upfront that I can't prevent drift — no registry or compatibility rule reaches into a vendor's API. So the strategy shifts from prevention to fast detection and contained blast radius.

Concretely: I'd validate every incoming payload against the schema I expect at the moment of ingestion, and fail loudly or quarantine the specific batch rather than letting a shape change silently flow through — a field that silently becomes null instead of a number is far worse than a job that stops and pages someone, because the silent version corrupts downstream aggregates before anyone notices. I'd also always land the raw, unmodified payload in a bronze/raw layer before any parsing happens, so if my typed model didn't anticipate a new field or a changed type, I still have the original data to reprocess once I fix the parser — nothing is lost, only delayed.

On the defensive-coding side, I'd treat every field's type as best-effort rather than guaranteed: coerce with explicit fallback logic instead of assuming a `price` field will always be a number, and add monitoring on parse-failure rate and unexpected-field counts so a vendor's silent change shows up as a metric spike within minutes, not as a wrong number in a report weeks later.

I'd also keep a lightweight contact or changelog-subscription with the vendor where possible, since detection is a backstop — an actual heads-up beats detecting the change after it's already happened.

**Testing:** whether you can design for a source you don't control, rather than assuming registry-style enforcement is always available.
